slides.text: This course is a first introduction to probability, written with science and engineering students in mind. We begin with the basic language of the subject: sample spaces and events, and the axioms that every probability must satisfy. From there we move on to conditional probability, independence, and Bayes' theorem, which tell us how to update probabilities when we learn new information. Later we turn to discrete random variables and two of their most important summaries, expectation and variance. To keep things concrete, each chapter ends with a short worked example, so you can see the ideas applied to an actual calculation before moving on.

With that roadmap in mind, let's start with the most basic building blocks, sample spaces and events. A random experiment is any process whose outcome cannot be predicted with certainty, such as tossing a coin or measuring how long a light bulb lasts. The sample space, which we call S, is the set of all possible outcomes. For a single roll of a die, S is the set containing one, two, three, four, five and six. An event is simply a subset of the sample space. For example, the event "the roll is even" is A equals the set two, four, six. We say an event occurs when the actual outcome belongs to it. The empty set can never occur, so it is the impossible event, while S itself always occurs, so it is the certain event.

Now that we know what events are, we can combine them to build new ones. The union of A and B is the event that A or B occurs, meaning at least one of them. The intersection of A and B is the event that both occur. The complement of A is the event that A does not occur. Two events are called mutually exclusive, or disjoint, if they cannot occur together, which means their intersection is empty. Let's see this with a die. Take A to be "the roll is even" and B to be "the roll is greater than three". Their union is the set two, four, five, six, and their intersection is the set four, six, the outcomes that are both even and larger than three.

Having described events, we now need a way to attach numbers to them, and that brings us to the axioms of probability. A probability measure assigns a number, P of A, to every event A. Kolmogorov's axioms say what rules these numbers must follow. First, probabilities are never negative, so P of A is greater than or equal to zero. Second, the probability of the whole sample space is one: P of S equals one, since the certain event always happens. Third, for mutually exclusive events, probabilities add. In symbols, P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B, whenever A intersect B is the empty set. In words, for disjoint events, the probability that one or the other occurs is just the sum of their probabilities.

From these three simple axioms, several useful rules follow. The complement of A has probability one minus P of A. The impossible event, the empty set, has probability zero. And for any two events, not necessarily disjoint, we have the general addition rule: P of A union B equals P of A plus P of B minus P of A intersect B. The reason for subtracting is that outcomes in the overlap would otherwise be counted twice, so we add the probabilities and remove the double-counted part. A very common special case is when all outcomes are equally likely. Then the probability of an event is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the total number of outcomes. For a fair die, the probability of an even roll is three over six, which is one half.

So far our probabilities assumed we knew nothing about the outcome. We now turn to conditional probability and independence, which describe how the probability of an event changes when we know another event has occurred. The probability of A given B is defined as P of A intersect B divided by P of B. In words, it is the probability that both occur, divided by the probability of B. This definition only makes sense when P of B is greater than zero. If we rearrange it, we get the multiplication rule: P of A intersect B equals P of A given B times P of B. This rule is often the easiest way to compute the probability that two things both happen.

Building on conditional probability, we get two important tools. The first is the law of total probability. If we split the sample space into a partition of disjoint cases, B one through B n, then P of A equals the sum, for i from one to n, of P of A given B i times P of B i. So the probability of A is a weighted sum of its conditional probabilities over all the cases. The second idea is independence. Two events are independent if knowing that one occurred does not change the probability of the other. Equivalently, P of A intersect B equals P of A times P of B. Be careful: independence is not the same as mutual exclusivity. Disjoint events with positive probabilities are always dependent, because if one occurs, the other cannot.

To close this chapter, let's apply the multiplication rule to a concrete example. Suppose we draw two cards from a standard deck, without replacement. What is the probability that both are aces? The first card is an ace with probability four over fifty-two. Then we multiply by three over fifty-one, giving about zero point zero zero four five. Notice that the second factor is a conditional probability: given that the first card was an ace, it has been removed, so only three aces remain among fifty-one cards. This is exactly the multiplication rule at work, P of both equals P of the second given the first, times P of the first.

Having worked through conditional probabilities like the two aces example, we can now turn the question around. Bayes' theorem reverses a conditional probability. It lets us express the probability of B given A using the probability of A given B, which is often the quantity that is easier to know. The formula says: the probability of B given A equals the probability of A given B, times the probability of B, all divided by the probability of A. In words, the posterior probability of B given A equals the likelihood of A given B times the prior of B, divided by P of A. We call P of B the prior probability, our belief before seeing A, and P of B given A the posterior probability, our belief after seeing A. The denominator, P of A, is usually computed with the law of total probability.

To see Bayes' theorem in action, consider a medical test. Suppose a disease affects one percent of the population. The test detects ninety-nine percent of sick people, but it also gives false positives for five percent of healthy people. What is the probability that someone is actually sick, given a positive result? Applying Bayes, the numerator is zero point nine nine times zero point zero one. The denominator adds the false positives: zero point nine nine times zero point zero one, plus zero point zero five times zero point nine nine. The result is only about zero point one seven, roughly seventeen percent. Why so low? Because the prior is so small that most positive results are false positives. The healthy majority generates more false alarms than the sick minority generates true detections.

So far we have worked with probabilities of events; now we attach numbers to outcomes. A random variable is a function assigning a number to each outcome. It is discrete when it takes a finite or countable number of values. Its probability mass function, written p of x, gives the probability that the variable equals x; these values are non-negative and sum to one. The expectation is a probability-weighted average: E of X equals the sum over all x of x times p of x, so each value is weighted by its probability. The variance measures the spread around the mean. A convenient formula is: the variance of X equals E of X squared minus the square of E of X. In other words, the mean of the square minus the square of the mean.

With mean and variance defined, let's see how they behave under simple transformations. Expectation is linear: E of a X plus b equals a times E of X, plus b, for any constants a and b. Scaling and shifting a random variable scales and shifts its mean in the same way. For variance, the variance of a X plus b equals a squared times the variance of X. Scaling multiplies the variance by the square of the factor, while adding a constant does not change the spread at all. Now a fair die. E of X is one plus two up to six, divided by six, which gives three point five. The expected square, E of X squared, is ninety-one sixths. So the variance is ninety-one sixths minus three point five squared, which is twelve point two five, giving about two point nine two.
